title: The serpent who teaches the seat
hookLine: the serpent who holds up Vishnu comes down as a teacher, and starts with how to sit
carry: posture and breath are rungs toward a still mind
tomorrow: who taught yoga first, and who overheard?

cards: Out on the cosmic ocean, Vishnu rests on a great serpent with a thousand heads. Its name is Shesha, also called Ananta, the endless. It holds him steady, coiled and at ease, through the long night between worlds.
Tradition tells that this serpent once came down to teach. A woman named Gonika stood praying with her palms cupped, and a tiny snake dropped into them.

He grew up to be Patanjali, the teacher of the Yoga Sutras; tradition hears his name as fallen, pata, into folded palms, anjali. Today: what he teaches about sitting, breathing, and what both are for.

teach.b: That's a legend from later tradition; the Sutras never tell his life. But notice what it makes of him: the serpent who is God's own couch becomes the teacher of the seat.

Patanjali opens with yoga's aim, in paraphrase: yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind, and then the seer rests in its own nature. That's the big teaching. In Hindu yoga the goal isn't a body.
It's a mind quiet enough for the self, the seer, to be seen. To get there he lays out eight limbs, ashtanga. First, how you treat others and yourself.
Then posture, then breath, and on up to meditation and absorption.
Posture and breath are rungs three and four. Now the seat.

teach.h: A STEADY, EASY SEAT; THEN A PAUSE
teach.b: Patanjali asks for one that is steady and easy, sthira and sukha. It comes, he says, as effort loosens and the mind rests on the endless, ananta.
Some teachers hear the serpent's own name in that word: sit the way Ananta holds Vishnu, firm and at ease. That's a reading, not the text.
Only after the seat comes pranayama, which he defines as a pause in the flow of breathing in and breathing out. Not a push. Its fruit: the mind becomes fit for concentration.
Some yoga classes open with a chant bowing to Patanjali as that white, thousand-headed serpent. They're borrowing a ladder whose top is the self.

teach.h: THE STRETCH IS A LOW RUNG
teach.b: So when a class feels like a workout, remember: the stretch is a low rung, and the climb is toward a quiet mind. If you have heart or lung trouble, or get dizzy, keep breath practice gentle and ask a doctor first.

how: In yoga traditions that follow Patanjali, posture and breath come after ethical restraints and observances and lead toward concentration and meditation; some classes open with an invocation to Patanjali, pictured as the serpent Adishesha.

games.q: you're Patanjali, laying out yoga's ladder. what is the whole climb for?
o: a mind still enough for the seer to rest in itself.
breath you can hold longer than anyone.
games.why: yoga is the stilling of the mind's movements, and then the seer rests in its own nature. posture and breath serve that.

practice: Sit the way the serpent holds Vishnu: steady first, then easy, shoulders down, jaw loose, effort loosening a little with each breath out.
Only then turn to the breath, and don't steer it; if a natural little pause comes after a breath out, notice it without stretching it, and if anything strains, go back to the seat.
If you pray, you can let the stillness be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: The breath again. In Patanjali, a steady, easy seat comes first, and pranayama is a pause in the flow of breath, both rungs toward a still mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the breath practice of the Yoga Sutras, defined there as a pause in the flow of breathing in and out.

carryVoice: Your line: posture and breath are rungs toward a still mind. Patanjali's ladder ends in the self. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 1.2–1.3 (yoga is the stilling of the movements of the mind; then the seer rests in its own nature)
Yoga Sutras 2.46–2.49 (a steady, easy seat; effort loosened, the mind resting on the endless; then pranayama, the pause in the flow of in-breath and out-breath)
Yoga Sutras 2.52–2.53 (the covering of the light thins; the mind fit for concentration)
